title: Reading code and conditional statements
text: Tuesday we ran code and thought about the results, today we are going to focus on how read and understand the code without needing to run it. Included is an example of the spec → prompt → annotate → verify process. Then we go through conditional statements, which bring us to the interesting and sometimes-confusing world of branching logic: if something is True, do this, but if False, do something else.

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
Think First
Recall

From Tuesday: what does = actually do, and why is count = count + 1 not nonsense?
From week 1: what fills the gaps in an under-specified prompt?

Look Ahead

Could you convince someone a program is correct without running it?
What’s the difference between a comment that says what a line does and one that says why it’s there?
What does it mean for a program to “choose” between two different things to do — and how would you trace that choice by hand?

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
The reading vocabulary
You already know enough Python to read most short engineering scripts. Here’s a beginning inventory:


Truthfully, much of what I code is handling arithmetic — nothing fancy at all. Take these numbers, square them and multiply by this constant, and plot the result. You don’t know plotting yet, but you are quickly learning to understand how math is represented in code.



You see
It means




x = 5
store 5 under the name x (“x is assigned 5”)


print(x)
display the value of x


x ** 2, x / y
power, division


# text
code comments

title: Reading code and conditional statements
section: Tracing: running code in your head
text:
Tracing: running code in your head
To trace a program, be the computer: go top to bottom, one line at a time, keeping a little table of every variable’s current value. (Run the code after your trace to confirm your suspicions.)












NoteClick to see the trace





After line 1: a = 2, with b and c not yet defined. After line 2: a = 2, b = 5. After line 3: a = 20, b = 5. After line 4: c = 25.



Tracing is slow and that’s fine — it’s a verification strategy you’ll only deploy on the sections you aren’t sure about

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
Annotation
When an AI hands you code, you will annotate it. That’s not the same as reading the comments the AI already left, it means writing, in your own words, what every line or logical block does and why it’s there. Producing that explanation yourself, not just reading someone else’s, is what actually proves you understand the code.






Important



Rule 1: A line you can’t annotate is a line you do not understand.
Rule 2: Annotate the why, not just the what. # convert to liters is better than # multiply by 1000. (The latter is probably a repeat of the code!)

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
One full lap: the 3D-printer problem
The problem: How much filament will it take to 3D-print this part?
Step 1 — Specification. Inputs — part volume (cm³), infill fraction (0–1), filament diameter (mm). Output — filament length needed, in meters. Assumptions — filament is drawn out as a solid cylinder, no waste from priming or purge lines, infill fraction distributed uniformly. Edge cases — zero diameter will raise a division-by-zero error rather than silently returning a bad result.


The slicer is the software that turns a 3D model into printing instructions. The infill fraction is the fraction of a part’s interior that is plastic — if its value is, say, 0.20, the interior of an apparently solid object is a lattice that is 20% plastic and 80% air.
Step 2 — The prompt. The spec practically is the prompt:

Write a Python script that computes the length of filament needed to 3D-print a part. Inputs: part volume in cubic centimeters, infill fraction (0 to 1), and filament diameter in millimeters. Output the filament length in meters including units. Comment each step, including tracking the units/unit conversions along the way.

Step 3 — Annotate what comes back. Suppose the AI returns:






Some initial good news: the code runs without any error messages, and every line is commented and makes sense. We’ve annotated three lines… these are worth checking: are the conversions and equations correct? They are chances for a silent error that would deliver an incorrect output!


You don’t necessarily need to comment every line, especially if the variable names are intuitive. You also might be able to comment on an entire block at once, or if there are repeated steps just describe the first one, or … . Just make sure your code+comments is understandable!
Step 4 — Verify. Hand estimate: the printed volume is \(45 \times 0.20 = 9\) cm³ = 9,000 mm³. The filament’s cross-section is roughly \(\pi (0.875)^2 \approx 2.4\) mm². So the required length is \(\approx 9{,}000 / 2.4 \approx 3{,}750\) mm \(\approx 3.75\) m. We were careful with units here, good. Edge case: set diameter = 0 and predict what happens before running.


You might ask: why did we write a program, and then calculate it by hand anyway? It’s good to have the confirmation — we might not trust the AI, and we might not trust our algebra, but if they agree we can feel better about both. But more importantly: we will get into functions next week, where we write code that can accept different input values, and maybe we use that function 1000 times on a project. With functions, we’ll check on one or two cases by hand, and if it’s good we can feel OK about using that function for the other 998 cases.

When the AI gets it plausibly wrong
The AI might return something like
volume_filled_mm3 = volume_filled_cm3 * 100    # convert cm^3 to mm^3
(E.g., centimeters to meters is a factor of 100… maybe it sees cm and conversion and assumes we are going that way.) It runs and reports a filament length of 0.37 m — maybe believable, but wrong by a factor of ten.

title: Reading code and conditional statements
text:
One more thing: if/elif/else
Code tracing through algebra, checking unit conversions and area equations, etc., is important but kind of boring. Let’s go ahead and introduce conditional statements in this reading: they lead to branching… the code takes different paths depending on whether a condition is True or False.

Conditions
Conditions are expressions that evaluate to either True or False. Very useful in coding, e.g. if we are doing a fluid mechanics calculation, the pressure-drop equation we use depends on whether the flow is laminar or turbulent. Our code might check “is the flow turbulent?” If False, it will proceed with the laminar equation; if True, it will proceed with the turbulent equation.
Here are examples of all six basic conditions:



Condition
Meaning




x == 5
“x is equal to 5”


b!=3
“b is not equal to 3”


a>3
“a is greater than 3”


a>=2
“a is greater than or equal to 2”


c<-99
“c is less than negative 99”


c<=8
“c is less than or equal to 8”





The double equals == is the “conditional equals”, the single equals = is the “assignment equals”. 5=3 will get you an error, but 5==3 will be interpreted as False, and the program will keep running no problem.
These conditions evaluate as either True or False:






Conditional statements can also be combined, and in Python it is really nice: we get to use the words and and or. Statements with and or or can still be evaluated as True or False


MATLAB, Java, C, C++, and others use && and || for “and” and “or”… not too bad, but not as readable as and and or!






and we can make it pretty complicated by combining these expressions!








if statements
These are very readable, so let’s just dive in with a basic example:






This is an if statement. If the condition described after the if is True, Python executes the code inside the block that follows; if it is False, it skips it.


In Python, a block is a collection of lines with the same amount of indent level. Python is a unique language in that it defines its blocks based on the indent — in other languages we enclose blocks in braces {} or maybe we introduce a block with an if and end it explicitly with a line that just says end. Many folks enjoy Python because it is uncluttered.






Warning



Python’s indented blocks are very nice, the code looks very clean, but you have to be accurate with your spacing. This is fine:






and this is fine






but this will break








Be alert for rogue spaces!


if/else statements
This is pretty intuitive as well:






This is an if/else statement: it checks the condition after the if and, if it’s true, it executes the code within the if block but not the code within the else block. If the condition after the if is false it skips the code within the if block and executes the code within the else block.


if/elif/else statements
A third structure:


In Python, elif is “else if”.






This is an if/else if/else statement: it checks the condition after the if and, if it is True, it executes the if block then skips the elif and else blocks. If the condition after the if is False, it checks the condition after the elif, and if that is True, it executes the elif block and skips the else block. If both the if and elif conditions are False, it executes the code within the else block.
I feel like explaining that in a paragraph might have been more confusing than just reading the code!






Important



You can add more than one elif. The conditions are always checked from top to bottom, and the first one that evaluates as True is the only part of the structure that is actually executed by Python.
It is not mandatory to have an else statement. If none of the if/elif conditions are True and there is no else, it is effectively the same as just skipping the whole block. Sometimes that is desired!




Nested conditional statements
By using two levels of indentation, we can create nested conditional statements. Try to understand the following…












Tip



If the if statement is false, we move on to the elif. If the elif statement is True, we execute its block. Within there, we’ve got another if to consider.


The hardest trace on this page!

Below is an AI-generated script with three planted flaws: one syntax error (won’t run), one loud error (runs, obviously wrong), and one silent error (runs, plausibly wrong). On paper: annotate every line, name all three flaws, trace the if statement and say whether its warning prints, and state what the correct filament length should be. Don’t run it first, you are here to learn!
import math

diameter     = 1.75    # filament diameter, mm
part_volume  = 45      # part volume, cm^3
infill       = 0.20    # fraction of volume actually printed
spool_volume = 285     # cm^3 of plastic on a standard 1 kg spool

volume_filled = part_volume * infill      # cm^3 of plastic actually extruded
volume_mm3    = volume_filled * 1000      # convert cm^3 to mm^3
area          = math.pi * diameter ** 2   # cross-sectional area of filament, mm^2
length_mm     = area / volume_mm3         # mm of filament needed
length_m      = length_mm / 1000          # convert mm to m

if volume_filled > spool_volume:
    print("warning: volume larger than standard spool size")

print("Filament needed:", length_m "m")





We’re building a collection of error messages. In class on Tuesday we encountered NameError (used a variable name Python has never seen before), SyntaxError (the code is not valid Python — it can’t run), and TypeError (e.g., we tried to do math with data that was interpreted as text: in 5+“15”, the 15 is text). Setting diameter = 0 back in Step 4 gives a ZeroDivisionError (you asked Python to divide by zero). When we had inconsistent indentation in the if block, we got an IndentationError.

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text: You will use AI consistently in this course and you might have some experience already. (If not, don’t worry!) Let’s spend one lesson on what’s it’s actually doing.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
Think First
Recall

Your phone’s keyboard suggests the next word as you type. How do you think it decides what to suggest?
Have you ever confidently “remembered” something that turned out to be wrong?

Look Ahead

If two students give an AI the exact same prompt, will they get the exact same code back?
Why might an AI be better at writing code than at doing arithmetic?
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
The short version
A large language model (LLM) does one thing:

Given some text, predict a plausible next small chunk of text.

That’s it. Everything else — the code-writing, the explanations, the apparent reasoning — emerges from doing that one thing extremely well, at enormous scale.


The “small chunks” are called tokens — usually a word or piece of a word. thermal might be one token; thermodynamics might be three. (Different than the tokens involved in our standards-based grading scheme!)
The model learned to do this by, in effect, reading a colossal amount of text — books, articles, documentation, and importantly for us, billions of lines of code — and adjusting billions (perhaps trillions) of internal numerical knobs until its “next-chunk” predictions got very good. This is what we mean when we talk about a new LLM “model” — there are more parameters (knobs) and updated tunings of those knobs that do a better job of creating accurate/plausible bodies of text.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
text:
Three consequences
Everything strange about LLM behavior falls out of that mechanism.

1. Its answers are plausible, but might not be true
The model produces text that is statistically likely to follow your prompt — the text sounds like what the correct answer might sound like. It is not reasoning based on physics, it has read a bunch of text written by humans who reasoned based on physics. Then it realized, statistically, that whenever those humans mention “physics”, “black holes”, and “singularity”, it is probably appropriate to use the word “Hawking”, and a likely word after that is “radiation”.


One concerning thing about LLMs is that they are increasingly being trained on text generated by LLMs — so much internet content is generated by LLMs that the LLMs are reinforcing their own tendencies and possibly that will lead to quality degrading over generations.
Usually, the most plausible continuation of an engineering question is the correct answer, which is why these tools are often useful. But when the model doesn’t “know,” it does not stop and say so. It keeps generating plausible text — a medical treatment suggestion that doesn’t apply to the situation (dangerous!), a citation to a paper that doesn’t exist, a recipe with a cup of vanilla instead of a teaspoon. This is often called a hallucination, and the dangerous part is that the LLM can be just as confident about a hallucination as it is about real information.






Important



There is no tone difference between an LLM being right and an LLM being wrong. Verify!




2. Same prompt, different answers
Prediction produces a menu of plausible next chunks, each with a probability. By design, the model doesn’t always pick the single most likely one. A bit of controlled randomness in the choice makes output more varied and, usually, better. Run the same prompt twice and the choices fork somewhere, and once forked, the two continuations keep diverging.


LLMs with a higher “temperature” value (not the physical temperature) are more likely to choose a token with a lower probability. An LLM with zero temperature chooses the most probable token every time — for a given prompt, it creates the same output every time.
This is why, on Thursday, 15 tables prompting for the same task will produce 15 different programs — different variable names, different structures, sometimes different algorithms, occasionally different answers. Thinking about that is an important aspect of this class!


3. A good specification tames the LLM
A prompt is the text you supply to the LLM, maybe a question. An effective prompt is thoughtful… it’s not like a Google search where you just say some relevant words (“lyrics steely dan”) and then you, yourself, look through the results to find what you are looking for. You should be supplying instructions, relevant context, and constraints.


Does anyone else find it annoying that Google’s first result is now AI? Whenever I don’t know exactly what I am looking for, being able to scan the first few results is usually what it takes to figure it out; and whenever I do know what I am looking for, I am not interested in Gemini’s mediocre summary!
“Build me a diet plan” is too general to be immediately useful… are you trying to lose weight? Gain weight? Gain muscle? Add more fiber? Eliminate carbs? Allergic to nuts? The LLM will probably follow up with questions like that, and you’ll end up somewhere good, but sometimes it might make assumptions for you that you have to spend time undoing. (“Yuck, it wants me to eat fish three times a week!”)
Rather than arguing with the LLM for 15 minutes, wasting a bunch of water and electricity in the process, you should be thoughtful about your specifications.


The context window is the cap on how much of that text the model can “see” at once — your current prompt, along with (at least some of) your previous questions in the same conversation, any files you’ve included. And maybe you’ve given the LLM some baseline instructions that are automatically applied to all conversations. There is a limit on how much of that information can be included in a given text-generation step, and even if it were all included, the more context it has, the greater chance of getting confused! I suspect part of the model development that is happening is about doing a better job understanding what in the context window is most relevant to your current prompt.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
section: Why is it so good at code, anyway?
text:
Why is it so good at code, anyway?
The biggest reason: the training data included billions of lines of code, much of it from working programs, and a lot of solid documentation from the code creators themselves ( find_peaks). So there is a strong statistical signal that these are very relevant words for this task.
But furthermore: code is checkable. Compare

“You can’t fix every problem, so just focus on doing good work in your own corner of it.”

with

“It is not our part to master all the tides of the world, but to do what is in us for the succour of those years wherein we are set, uprooting the evil in the fields that we know, so that those who live after may have clean earth to till.”

How can you judge that the first one is “wrong”? Based on our understanding of how LLMs work, every new word/token in that line is a completely reasonable continuation of the sentence. The second one, by Tolkien, is better, but not “more correct”.
Meanwhile: if code doesn’t run, something is wrong, and we further will get an output from code that can possibly be confirmed/validated against known results. Modern LLMs are able to run code on the cloud to confirm they perform as intended, and they are increasingly willing to compare against test cases for you: if you need some code to find the area under a curve, an LLM might write it, run it, and compare against the known area under \(y=x\) from 0 to 1. Basically, the LLMs are doing their own small verification. That probably isn’t sufficient to confirm that the code does what it is supposed to, but it is necessary that the code works for at least that basic problem.
We will do our own audit and verification of the code: read through it to make sure it follows a logic we agree with, and test its output in several ways. We may need to iterate — the AI gives us code that seems like it is 90% of the way to succeeding at the job, but there is an error, and so we need to work with the AI to revise. Unlike prose, we can identify specifics about what is wrong and eventually arrive at something that is verified correct.


Meanwhile: LLMs are historically mediocre at arithmetic — predicting a text representation of numbers in a calculation is not the same as calculating.
crumbs: What does an LLM actually do?

title: What does an LLM actually do?
section: The stance on LLMs in this course
text:
The stance on LLMs in this course
No doubt, LLMs are tools that can augment your abilities. A few years ago I might have manually combined 40 spreadsheets into one (which maybe would have taken an hour, but was annoying), or I might have written code to do that for me (which probably would have taken four hours to figure out… should have just done it manually arggg). Now I can ask an LLM to give me the Python code to do it, and the project is done in 5 minutes.
I have become more ambitious and capable in some aspects of my work because I know I can get a head start using AI. But note: I am the one who came up with the idea, and I needed to describe the problem and some of the necessary steps. And, importantly, I am the one responsible if something breaks along the way, and so I need to have a strategy to confirm that everything made it into the finished project successfully.
I think the following is very much in the spirit of coding in 2026: Think of LLMs as your extremely fast, extremely well-read, overconfident junior collaborator. You can use them to quickly retrieve information, you can ask them to help you write code, they can help troubleshoot problems. But ultimately, you are setting the expectations (specifications), and you are responsible for the project (so you better do some verification). And, further, there will be times when you have to show that you, too, actually know how to do the stuff (the checkpoints).


One more term you’ll see a lot: an agent is capable of actually making changes on your computer — creating new folders, creating/editing files, maybe sending emails — rather than giving you text in a web browser that you have to move around. Still basically a junior collaborator: you still provide the details and check the results, you just have to do less manual labor.

Answer these:

Two students give an LLM the identical prompt for a projectile program. Predict: (a) identical code, (b) different code, same numerical answers, (c) different code, possibly different answers. Write one sentence defending your pick.
The LLM hands you a projectile program and it runs without any errors, and produces a nice plot. List every distinct reason you can think of that its output might still be wrong.

title: Side Quests
text:
Once Base Camp winds down, Mondays keep going with a new flavor: Side Quests, for anyone who wants to go further than the course goes. Nothing here affects your grade, nothing is secretly required, nobody takes attendance — and by this point in the semester, Mondays are just the day we hang out and build things, which is roughly what engineering departments are for.
Dress rehearsals still claim the Mondays before checkpoints 3 and 4 (weeks 8 and 10); quests fill the rest. Which quests run is up to you — signups on Canvas; a quest runs if ~10 people want it — so consider this page a menu. Pitch new ones anytime; the best quests come from what you ask for. Every quest that runs leaves behind a one-page recipe on this site, so the menu grows into a library.

title: Side Quests
text:
The menu
Starting from scratch. (Timed for week 11, right before project launch.) The blank-page protocol: what to actually do when there’s no template, no starter code, and no instructions — which is your project in four days, and most of your career. The protocol is teachable: restate the problem in one sentence; name inputs and outputs; find the smallest version that could possibly work; build that; grow it. We’ll start something real from nothing, live, mistakes included.
Git & version control. (Week 12.) How real teams avoid final_v2_ACTUAL_final.py: commits, history, branches, and undo-anything confidence.
Build a tiny language model. You’ve directed LLMs all semester; now build the ancestor — a Markov text generator, ~30 lines. Feed it a book from Project Gutenberg, watch it babble plausibly.
Parametric design → 3D print. Code that generates geometry: a bracket with parameterized dimensions, swept over a design variable — and then we print the winner on the College’s machines. It’s HW 3’s parameter sweep made physical: the design space in your hand. (Print queue permitting.)

title: Getting going in your language
text: This page contains my recommendations for how to set up your programming environment. You can do this entire course in Google Colab and MATLAB Online — nothing to install, works on any machine. But at some point you might decide running Python/MATLAB on your own machine is a good idea. Programs run faster, you can see all the files in a project easier, and it just feels better to have everything in a real editor.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Python via Google Colab
Go to colab.research.google.com, sign in with your university Google account, click New notebook, and… that’s it. Python runs on Google’s computers; NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas are pre-installed. Notebooks are saved on your Google Drive. It is a little bit clumsy to handle files (e.g. a csv) but we will figure it out!


We’ll talk about how to import packages soon… engineers don’t use base Python much, we need to bring in some extra tools.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
Python on your machine
There are multiple avenues here, and if you are confident enough to find your own way (e.g., with pip), I believe in you. In general, there are two things you’ll need to do: install Python+a package manager, and install an editor.

Package manager
My recommendation is to install miniconda — NOT the full Anaconda (which you can find nearby if you really want to, but I’m not linking it).


The full Anaconda is attractive: it has everything you will need in one install, but also a lot of unnecessary stuff. I grew to hate the navigator and the way it insisted on cross-checking all the packages every time I updated, and so I “downgraded” to miniconda (which still cross-checks, but there are way fewer packages). Additionally, I am not fond of the IDEs (Integrated Development Environment) that come with Anaconda. I much prefer VS Code, which supports Jupyter Notebooks and has a GitHub integration.
Miniconda installs Python, but otherwise I think there are zero packages, so you’ll install what you need from the command line. NumPy, matplotlib, and pandas are necessary for this course; this page has the instructions. Note that miniconda still uses conda as the command.


What are “packages”? They are collections Python files that include useful Python functions that can be “called”. For example: someone has already written an implementation of the Trapezoid Rule for finding the area under a curve, and implemented it into the SciPy package. Now, instead of writing the code from scratch, you can just call that function with trapezoid(y) in your code.

pip is another package-management option — not that different from conda. If you have reason to go that way, do it; plenty of tutorials around.







Tip



Some other packages that might be worth installing:

Jupyter is a “notebook” environment that looks a lot like Colab.
Seaborn is built on-top of matplotlib… it makes really beautiful plots.
SciPy is a toolbox of numerical routines — differential equation solvers, integrators, etc. It is a very large package but has a lot of very good tools that are used in engineering.
Scikit-learn is a good machine learning toolbox, we might use it in a Machine Learning Side Quest.





Editor
For the editor, I recommend VS Code — it supports Jupyter notebooks (and it’s notebook interface is better than the default Jupyter interface), has an integrated terminal, and has GitHub integration. Install VS Code, then its Python and Jupyter extensions (VS Code will automatically offer to install them the first time you open a .py or .ipynb file).


GitHub is a website that hosts code projects (“repositories”) so you can save your work, track changes over time, and share it with others.
If you would like to install a different editor, and feel confident in doing so, go ahead! One example: Google Antigravity is apparently quite similar to VS Code. (I haven’t tried it yet!)






NotePython “environments” (optional reading)





Many serious programmers insist each project should have its own “environment” with a unique set of packages. For example, TensorFlow apparently does not play nice with NumPy version 2.0 or higher, and so folks who use TensorFlow will likely have an isolated environment for it where NumPy 1.9x is installed. (Even after reverting to NumPy 1.9x, I still couldn’t get TensorFlow to work, but that is beside the point!) For this class, it should not be a big deal to work entirely in the base environment.
If you do want to create separate environments, e.g., one for each project, you can. From the command line, you would start with something like conda create --name project1 and then conda activate project1 puts you in that environment, and then conda install numpy would get you numpy in just that environment. You need to install packages in each environment – if you have three environments set up on your machine, you might technically have NumPy installed three times.

title: Getting going in your language
text:
MATLAB (later in the semester)
As a CU student you have free access: create a MathWorks account with your CU email — instructions are here, under the student “How to get it.”
Once your account is tied to the school’s license, you can install desktop MATLAB or use MATLAB Online in the browser — students have used both, and you can hop back and forth. I like the immediacy of a local install and it runs a bit faster; Online gives you your code from any computer. For our purposes, either is fine.
Basic MATLAB is all this course needs; no toolboxes required. Later MCEN courses will have you using toolboxes like Simulink (used in System Dynamics) — you can add those anytime, no need to install now.
The MathWorks “MATLAB Onramp” tutorial — find it under Online Training at matlab.mathworks.com — is genuinely good and takes about two hours. We won’t be using MATLAB until the second half of the course.

No attendance is taken, nothing here affects your grade, but you will have a better grasp of the material at the end of each session. Plus, it’s a good way to meet some more people in the class and to talk to me/the TA!

title: Base Camp
text:
The sessions
BC1 (Week 1) · The computer itself, and how to talk about code. Before any coding: the computer itself. Browsers vs. apps, Colab login, where a downloaded file goes, folders, uploading to Colab, what “the cloud” means for your work. Then the second half: how to ask a question about code — the vocabulary (what do you call **, [], :?), the best way to ask a question: what I ran / what I expected / what I got instead.

Practice library (async Base Camp)

title: HW 1 · The grade calculator
text:
Note



I will add an example solution (to a different problem) soon!

title: HW 1 · The grade calculator
text:
Scenario
Build a program that tells a student their letter grade in this course.
Everything the program needs to know is on the grading page — standards, engagement credits, tokens, and the table summarizing how they translate to grades. Deciding what your program actually asks for is part of your job: read the grading page the way you’d read a client’s description of a problem, not a spec someone already wrote for you.

title: HW 1 · The grade calculator
text:
It’s trickier than it looks!
As you write your problem specifications, you’ll run into questions that require careful answers. What happens right at a threshold — 13 standards, or exactly 40 engagement credits? What does an unspent token do to that count, and when? If a student misses the D— row (an F, by the rules), and then somehow gives a distinguished final defense, does that do anything for them? (Our school does not grant F+ grades!) These are edge cases. If there is anything ambiguous, state your interpretation in the spec.

title: HW 1 · The grade calculator
text:
Your submission
Step 1 — Specify & prompt. Every input your program needs, in your own words — names, types, valid ranges — and where each one comes from on the grading page. Output format. Every edge case you dream up, each with your decision and a sentence of reasoning. This should be separate from your LLM prompt…
… but then also include your LLM prompt, which will indeed contain a lot of the same information. (See the example, when I post it.) Ask for a Python script: a handful of variables set at the top that you can edit by hand, the calculation, then a print of the result.
Step 2 — Annotate the returned code. For a line of the grade-table logic, say which case it’s catching and why it’s there. If you notice something the code decided that you never specified — an order of checks, an assumption — say so.
Step 3 — Verify. Hand-compute your predictions before you run anything, for at least four cases, and write them down first. Include at least one boundary-exact case (a student sitting precisely on a row’s threshold) and one that depends on token conversion — a student whose credit count only clears a threshold once their leftover tokens are added in. Report what actually happened, including anything that surprised you.
Step 4 — Report. One page: your spec, your four-plus test cases with results, your edge-case rulings, and one sentence on the ambiguity you found most interesting. Include the model, roughly when you ran it, and the prompt itself.

title: An example homework submission
text:
The problem
Here is a sign posted at the entrance of a parking garage.

MESA LOT — RATES

First 30 minutes: free
Up to 2 hours: $4
Up to 5 hours: $9
Over 5 hours: $16
Daily maximum: $16 — no vehicle is charged more than this in a 24-hour period
Overnight surcharge (vehicle present at 3:00 AM): add $10
Departmental validation: $3 off
Lost ticket: $25 flat


The gate machine records the time a car enters and the time it leaves, and the attendant can tell you whether the ticket was validated or lost. A driver pulls up to the exit. Write a program that determines what they owe.

title: An example homework submission
text:
Step 1 — Specification and prompt
What the program needs to know. Four things that I’ll provide at the top of the script: the time the car entered, the time it left, whether the ticket was validated, and whether it was lost.
The awkward decision is how to write a time. I settled on a plain number on a 24-hour clock, in decimal hours — so 11:15 PM is 23.25. Writing 2:30 PM as 14.5 is a little unnatural, and I could have used hours and minutes as separate variables, but then the arithmetic gets messy and I’d be doing conversions by hand every time I tested something.

Output. One number printed to the screen: the amount owed, in dollars, to the nearest cent.
Decisions I had to make, because the sign doesn’t say:








Situation
My ruling
Why




Exactly 0.5 hours
Free
Let’s hope it’s a friendly lot.


Exactly 2.0 hours
$4
Same logic, be consistent.


Overnight + the 5-hour rate = $26, above the daily max
Charge $26
The max is about parking rates; the surcharge is a penalty on top. Could go the other way, would need to clarify.


Validation and daily max together
Apply validation last, so $16 → $13
The discount is something the department gives you, so it should come off whatever you’d otherwise owe.


Lost ticket + validation
$25 − $3 = $22
The sign doesn’t exempt it.


Lost ticket + overnight
$25 flat, no surcharge
“Flat”.


Validation on a free stay
$0, never negative
“Parking garages hate this one trick” … program might return -$3!


Exit time equals entry time
Treat as an error and say so
Either they didn’t park or they stayed exactly 24 hours, and I can’t tell which. Not guessing.


Stay longer than 24 hours
Can’t be expressed with two clock times, so out of scope
A consequence of my input choice. If this mattered I’d need a date, not a time.


A time outside 0 to 24
Refuse, with an error
Not a real clock time — probably a typo.









TipCommentary



This table is a good chunk of the grade. Every row states a ruling, and in cases of ambiguity a choice is made. “I could see it going the other way” is a reasonable addition to your submission. Again, this errs on the side of being over-detailed (with 10 cases)… five cases would probably be enough.


My prompt.

Write a short Python script (not function, I haven’t learned those yet) that calculates what a driver owes at a parking garage. I want the input values as variables at the top of the script where I can edit them by hand, then the calculation, then a print of the result. Don’t ask for user input.
The variables at the top are time_in and time_out, each a number on a 24-hour clock in decimal hours (11:15 PM is 23.25), and validated and lost_ticket, each True or False.
A car may stay past midnight, so if time_out is less than or equal to time_in, add 24 to time_out before anything else. The duration is then time_out - time_in.
The car counts as overnight if it was in the lot at 3:00 AM — that is, if either 3 or 27 falls between time_in and time_out on that adjusted timeline.
Rate tiers by duration: 0 up to and including 0.5 hours is $0. Above 0.5 up to and including 2.0 hours is $4. Above 2.0 up to and including 5.0 hours is $9. Above 5.0 hours is $16.
Then: if overnight, add $10 — this is allowed to exceed the $16 daily maximum, because the maximum applies to the duration rate only. Then if validated is True, subtract $3, but never below $0.
If lost_ticket is True, the charge is $25 flat regardless of duration and regardless of overnight, but validation still applies, giving $22.
If either time is outside 0 to 24, or if time_out equals time_in, print a message explaining the problem instead of a price.
Print the final amount to the nearest cent, with a dollar sign.







TipCommentary



The prompt carries the rulings from the table into the request. It states the boundaries as “up to and including,” names the order of operations explicitly, and says what not to do. Compare it to what most people would send: a photograph of the sign and “write me a program for this.” That version outsources all ten decisions to the LLM, which will make them silently.
Two important lines: the midnight rule and the 3-or-27 condition. Neither is on the sign. The student worked out that “present at 3:00 AM” means an interval containing 3 o’clock, and that a car parked from 10 PM to 6 AM lives on a timeline where 3 AM is at hour 27 — and then said so. 
Note also the part about not using functions. An LLM would likely jump to using functions, which is something we don’t know yet — though you can use them, if you have some experience. Telling LLMs what you know is a legitimate and underused aspect of prompting.

title: An example homework submission
text:
Step 2 — Annotation
I’ve annotated the returned code in comments. A few lines I want to point out here:






NoteClick here for the full script the LLM gave me





This is what came back, before I fixed anything — the two bugs from Step 3 are both still in here if you want to hunt for them yourself.
# --- inputs, edit these by hand ---
time_in = 22.0        # 24-hour clock, decimal hours (11:15 PM = 23.25)
time_out = 4.0
validated = False
lost_ticket = False
# ----------------------------------

if time_in < 0 or time_in > 24 or time_out < 0 or time_out > 24:
    print("Error: times must be between 0 and 24.")
else:
    if time_out <= time_in:
        time_out = time_out + 24      # car crossed midnight

    if time_out == time_in:
        print("Error: entry and exit times are the same.")
    else:
        hours = time_out - time_in

        # was the car here at 3 AM? (3 on day one, 27 on day two)
        overnight = (time_in <= 3 <= time_out) or (time_in <= 27 <= time_out)

        if hours <= 0.5:
            fee = 0.0
        elif hours <= 2.0:
            fee = 4.0
        elif hours <= 5.0:
            fee = 9.0
        else:
            fee = 16.0

        if lost_ticket:
            fee = 25.0

        if overnight:
            fee = fee + 10.0

        if validated:
            fee = fee - 3.0
            if fee < 0:
                fee = 0.0

        print("Amount owed: $" + str(round(fee, 2)))



if time_out <= time_in:
    time_out = time_out + 24    # the car crossed midnight
This is important for an overnight stay — for a car in at 9 and out at 14, the if condition is false and the line is skipped entirely. After this runs, time_out can be 28, which is not a real clock time… which felt wrong, but after inputting decimal times, we start thinking about durations instead.






TipCommentary



This is a “tier three” (excellent) annotation — it doesn’t just say what the line does, it says the student noticed the result stopped looking like a clock time and had to work out why that’s still correct. Nothing in the code marks that shift, so catching it requires actually tracing the logic, not just reading each line in isolation.


if hours <= 0.5:
    fee = 0.0          # exactly 30 min is free
elif hours <= 2.0:
    fee = 4.0          # boundary at 2.0 goes to the cheap tier, as I asked
The elif chain is checked top to bottom and stops at the first true test, so a 0.4-hour stay never reaches the second line at all. That’s why the tiers can be written as simple <= comparisons without needing to say “and greater than 0.5” — the earlier branch already ate those cases.






TipCommentary



This one sits at “tier two” (good) — it’s more than a syntax gloss (“this is an elif”), since it explains why the comparisons can be written so simply. But it stops at describing the mechanism; it doesn’t flag anything the code decided that wasn’t asked for. Tier two is a perfectly acceptable annotation on its own — you don’t need tier three on every line — but a submission that never goes past tier two anywhere is probably not digesting the code completely.


if lost_ticket:
    fee = 25.0
This sits after the tier chain, so it overwrites whatever the duration produced. That’s correct behavior but it isn’t what I pictured — I imagined it checking the lost ticket first and skipping the tiers entirely.






TipCommentary



Tier three again. The discovery is about ordering — the code runs every branch and then overrides the result with a final if statement. Similar to the first annotation, the student noted a design choice the LLM made that the prompt did not specify and talked about it.
The three tiers of annotation are something like:

Restating the syntax (“this is an if statement”) is weakest.
Saying what a line does in the problem’s terms, like the elif note above, is fine.
Annotation that also notices something — an ordering, a hidden assumption, a variable that changed what it means — is great.

Not every single line needs to be the third tier.

Row four is the one I was most worried about and it’s fine: 10 PM to 4 AM, so through 3AM, and it ended up fine. Row nine checks the other 3 AM case — a car that arrives at 2 AM and leaves at 5 AM never crosses midnight at all, but is still there at 3 — and that works too.
Row eight is a real failure. My spec said a lost ticket is $25 flat regardless of overnight, and the prompt said so, but the if overnight block sits below the lost-ticket line and runs unconditionally, adding $10 to the flat charge. The model wrote the surcharge before it wrote the override and never reconciled them. I found it by testing combinations — lost alone passes, overnight alone passes, only the pair fails. The fix was moving the lost-ticket branch below the surcharge.
Row ten is subtler and it’s my own fault, not the model’s. I asked for an error when the times are equal, and I also asked for the add-24 rule when time_out <= time_in — and the add-24 rule is written first, so an 8-to-8 stay becomes a 24-hour stay, picks up the overnight surcharge on the way past 3 AM, and prints $26 before the error check ever runs. Two of my own requirements fighting each other. I moved the check above the wraparound.
One gripe: running ten cases meant editing four variables at the top and re-running the script ten times, then doing it all again after each fix. Thirty-odd edits and I lost my place twice. There has to be a better way to do this.






TipCommentary



This is the best part of the submission and it’s why the predictions have to be written before running. If you fill in the “I expect” column after seeing the output, you will be tempted to agree with the code. Also notice that the interaction bug — two features that are each fine alone and wrong together — is the kind an LLM produces constantly.

title: An example homework submission
text:
Step 4 — Report
What this does. Given when a car entered and left the Mesa Lot, whether the ticket was validated, and whether it was lost, this script prints what the driver owes. Times go in as decimal hours on a 24-hour clock, e.g. 11:15 PM is 23.25, and the script handles the midnight wraparound and the 3 AM surcharge question itself.
Where I had to decide. The sign leaves a lot open and I ruled on ten cases, listed in Step 1. The three that actually changed the answer: the overnight surcharge stacks on top of the $16 daily maximum, validation comes off last so it applies to whatever you’d otherwise owe, and a lost ticket is $25 flat but still takes the $3 validation discount. I also put anything past 24 hours out of scope, which is a consequence of feeding the program clock times instead of dates.
What went wrong. Two bugs. The model’s: a lost ticket picked up the overnight surcharge anyway, because the surcharge line sits below the override and runs unconditionally — it output $35 where I’d predicted $25. Mine: I asked for an error when the times are equal and for the wraparound whenever time_out <= time_in, and the wraparound runs first, so an 8-to-8 stay quietly became a 24-hour stay and printed $26 instead of an error. Both were one-line moves. The second one is the one is harder to notice.
Provenance. Claude Sonnet 4.6, prompted 4 September 2026; the full prompt is in Step 1 and the returned code is folded into Step 2.






TipCommentary



Four short paragraphs: no abstract, no restated rate table, no walkthrough of the code. The report points at the other steps rather than repeating them — “the three that actually changed the answer” instead of the full list of ten.
You don’t want this to be too long — shorter than the specification. The test to apply: could a classmate who never saw the sign read this and know what the program does, what you decided, and what they’d need to rerun it?

title: Welcome
text:
Welcome to MCEN 1030: Introduction to Engineering Computing, taught by Professor Jeremy Koch in the Fall 2026 semester.
When I took this course (in Fall 2006… oof), the big challenge for students was to figure out how to use fundamental programming ideas — loops, conditional statements, indexing — to achieve an engineering task. My professor gave very clean problem statements so that we could focus on writing the code, and we spent hours figuring out how to put the ideas in the right order, getting the syntax right, and debugging errors.
Today, we have AI (artificial intelligence), specifically LLMs (large language models). These have proven to be extremely capable of writing code based on a prompt (natural language instructions). Engineers need some understanding of how computation can be used in their projects, but they are not manually typing in for i in items: anymore… they are writing prompts that include something like “iterate through the items in that list” and having an LLM do the work.
What does that mean for an introduction to engineering computing class, if traditional problems have been conquered by AI? We still need to learn what is possible with computation…
how computer logic works…
and how to interpret code…
but we will also learn how to integrate LLMs into our workflow. Importantly, we are not going to treat LLM-generated code as a “black box”1: we need to understand what is going on in our code. After all, if you end up using an LLM-generated result in your job and something explodes, you won’t be able to blame an LLM — it’s your fault!
Further, we’ll learn why LLMs are not 100% trustworthy and will see that they, too, often produce broken code. That doesn’t mean we give up on the project — if we understand how to talk about computational ideas, how to interpret results, and how to troubleshoot/debug, we can work with an LLM. The net effect will likely be that we produce better work, faster, as long as we humans are an active participant in the process.

title: Welcome
text:
The big idea
The process of creating computational tools looks roughly like this:

  The computational pipeline
  Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.
  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Idea
    
    Specification
    
    Production
    
    Verification
    
    Use
    
    
    
    
    
    Adaptation
  

For decades, Production — thinking about the code elements, structure, and syntax, and doing the typing — was the bottleneck, and so intro courses like this one spent nearly all their time on it. That bottleneck is gone: AI tools produce working code (from a good description) in seconds. The new bottlenecks are the two highlighted boxes:
Specification means describing the problem precisely: the inputs and outputs, what has to happen in the middle, what to do at the edges. If you can’t articulate the problem, no tool — human or AI — can solve it for you.
Verification means refusing to trust a black box: sanity-checking results against hand estimates, testing edge cases, knowing the ways a program (or a model, or an AI) goes wrong.
You will still read and run and modify plenty of code in this course — you can’t verify what you can’t read. But you will be graded on whether you can think computationally: frame a problem, direct the tools, and audit the results. That is what engineers actually do!

title: Welcome
text:
How a week works
Before class, you’ll read one lesson on this site (~20 minutes). Most of the code on these pages executes right in your browser and is editable. Every lesson ends with a Bring to class box: one question you answer on paper before you arrive.



More serious coding will happen in Google Colab, MATLAB Online, or Python/MATLAB on your own machine — the getting going page has instructions.
Class time is mostly group work at the tables. Early in the semester, mostly short problems with right answers. Later it shifts toward open-ended problems with design thinking. The readings introduce the concepts, and in class you’ll actually implement them.
Get extra practice on Mondays (optional). Base Camp early (the beginner on-ramp, checkpoint practice, …), Side Quests later (build a tiny language model, 3D-print a parameter sweep, …). No grades attached.
Checkpoints happen on Tuesdays (weeks 4, 6, 8, 10): twenty-minute “mini-exams”, individual, on paper, with no AI. See the grading page.
Homework problems are mostly about real mechanical engineering and will be formatted to include four steps: specify, annotate, verify, report. The homework page explains the format.

title: Welcome
text:
AI policy
You are expected to use AI tools in this course. You are also completely responsible for everything they produce for you. Every assignment asks you to show your specification, annotate the generated code, and demonstrate your verification.

title: Welcome
text:
Grading
This course uses standards-based grading, based on:

a list of specific skills (the standards), each marked Met or Not Yet
and engagement credits for preparation and in-class work.

There is no partial credit, no point-scrounging, and no penalty for struggling early: you can demonstrate a standard later when it reappears, and your grade is where you end up, not where you started. See the grading page.

title: Welcome
text:
Where to go next
Your first reading (for Tuesday) is What do engineers do with computation? You might look at Base Camp if you are new to coding and a bit nervous — the first few sessions designed to start you on the right foot. Try the Practice Library if you want to run some code right now in your browser (and let me know if it doesn’t work). If curious, you might browse the Side Quests — a few ideas are already on that page.

title: How your grade works
text:
Your grade is built from two ingredients, plus the final exam modifier:
Those two set a floor for your letter grade. The final exam — a written defense of your own project — then decides where inside that letter you land.
There are no points, no weighted averages, no partial credit, and no curve. Maybe most interesting: you can recover if you struggle early and still receive an A grade!

title: How your grade works
text:
Standards: the concepts
Every standard gets multiple opportunities across the semester. The rules:

Convergent standards (the ones with checkable right answers) require two successful demonstrations on different occasions.
Divergent standards (open-ended) require one demonstration at “Meets” quality, with the right to revise and resubmit once per artifact.
“Not Yet” means you aren’t there yet. But if you are Not Yet on a standard in week 4, then successfully demonstrate it in week 11, the standard is Met and you will receive full credit. (Though don’t forget convergent standards require two successful demonstrations.)
Reassessment happens at the scheduled reappearances of each standard, plus token-purchased retries — see Tokens.


Checkpoints
Four Tuesday classes (weeks 4, 6, 8, and 10) begin with a checkpoint: about twenty minutes, individual, on paper, no AI, no notes. Each checkpoint assesses a few convergent standards and re-offers items from earlier checkpoints. At least one of a convergent standard’s two demonstrations must be in-class. 

Expect to produce a short function by hand from a given spec — five lines or so, no AI. Why, in a course that delegates production to LLMs, are we having you write code yourself from scratch? Because verification requires an understanding of coding elements and at least a bit of fluency with the language.

title: How your grade works
text:
Engagement credits: the process
Part of your grade will be based on before-class preparation and in-class collaboration. These won’t be graded on correctness, and instead are based on good-faith completion:

Rules: a wrong answer with detailed reasoning earns full credit; a blank or a transparently rushed scribble earns none. Credits are earned in class and can’t be replaced with out of class work (though you can safely miss a few, and tokens can be used to make up some credits).

title: How your grade works
text:
Tokens
Everyone starts the semester with 3 tokens. Spend one for: a 48-hour deadline extension; an excused activity (the engagement credits without attending — illness, interviews, etc.); or one extra reassessment of a convergent standard outside its scheduled windows. No questions asked, no documentation required. Unspent tokens convert to 1 engagement credit each at semester’s end.

The final exam

The final is a written defense of your own project, assessed as:

title: How your grade works
text:
Three worked examples
Student 1 — the straightforward case. Meets 13 standards, earns 43 engagement credits, spends one token on an extension during a tough midterm week. Check the A- row: 13 ≥ 13 ✓, 43 ≥ 40 ✓ → floor of A-. Then the final: we might ask to trace the path the data takes through the functions and how something is filtered out, and let’s say Student 1 answers that well → solid → Grade: A.


For Student 1, the two unspent tokens add 2 credits (45), but that doesn’t change anything about the grade.
Student 2 — the slow start (read this one if you’re nervous). Bombs the first checkpoint, messing up two standards. No big deal — both are re-offered at the week-6 and week-8 checkpoints, and after also succeeding at them in the homework, Student 2 demonstrates each twice by mid-semester. Finishes with 11 standards Met. Then 41 engagement credits, having done the work all semester even while the checkpoints were rough. B- row: 11 ≥ 11 ✓, 41 ≥ 32 ✓ → floor of B-. Note that those 41 credits clear the A- row’s bar, but 11 standards don’t — the floor is the highest row where every requirement is met. Then the defense: Student 2 knows everything about the project, teammates’ files included → distinguished → Grade: B+.
Student 3 — the ghost (read this one if you’re planning to skip class). Brilliant, and knows it: 12 standards Met, some on first attempt. But treats class as optional — skips the readings’ commitments, misses most Thursdays — and finishes with 22 engagement credits, having spent no tokens (which convert: 22 + 3 = 25). A- row: 12 < 13 ✗. B- row: 12 ≥ 11 ✓, but 25 < 32 ✗. C- row: 12 ≥ 9 ✓, 25 ≥ 24 ✓ → floor of C-. The defense is, predictably, excellent → distinguished → Grade: C+. Is that harsh for someone with 12 standards and a great defense? Well, this course is also about the process — prepare, commit, argue, critique. Ten more Thursdays of just participating and we would be at a B+.

title: Practice Library
text:
Loops (week 5)
X1. Fix the loop so it prints the sum of the squares of 1 through 4. (What value do you expect?)







Run it as-is and look at what you get: 16. The loop isn’t accumulating — each pass throws away the previous total. What’s missing from the right-hand side?


total = total + k * k
The accumulator pattern: the new total is built from the old total. total = k * k just overwrites, and you end up with only the last pass (16).

X2. Assembly problem: these lines compute the average of a list, but they’re scrambled. Reorder them (cut and paste in the editor) so it runs and prints 5.0.








Names must exist before they’re used.
The indented line belongs to the for.
The print needs everything finished.

(Also — could you avoid hard-coding count = 3? Python’s len(values) exists and is probably better.


values = [3, 5, 7]
total = 0
count = 3
for v in values:
    total = total + v
print(total / count)
The first three lines can go in any order among themselves.

title: Practice Library
text:
Arrays (weeks 5–6)
A1. Fill in the blank so t holds the fall time for every height at once, then print it.







The formula is \(t=\sqrt{2h/g}\), and NumPy’s square root is np.sqrt(...). Write the arithmetic as if h were a single number — the array handles the “for every value” part itself.


t = np.sqrt(2 * h / 9.81)
The first entry should be ≈ 0.45 s and each height is 4× the previous, so each time should be 2× the previous (√4 = 2).

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text: We’re starting with computational thinking, not coding. What is actually possible with computation? What does a computer need from you to do something useful? How can you tell if a calculation is trustworthy? These are things we’ll be thinking about all semester, but we’ll introduce them here.
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
Think First
Recall

Think of a time you gave someone instructions (directions to your house, a recipe, rules to a game) and they got it wrong. Whose fault was it?
In high school physics, you checked answers by asking “is this number reasonable?” — a car going 900 m/s is probably a mistake. What was that process like… what were you recalling, what did you do when you realized the answer was ridiculous?

Look Ahead

If an AI can write working code from a plain-English description in five seconds, what’s left for the engineer to do?
What would it take for you to trust a program you didn’t write?
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Four things you may not know are possible with computation
text:
Four things you may not know are possible with computation
Predict every outcome of a process. Write a function that models something — the stress in a bracket, the temperature of a battery — then use that function 100 times with 100 different inputs and write every result to a file. Runtime: about one second. You have just explored the entire design space of a product before building anything.


A function has a very similar meaning in this class as it did in algebra: there are inputs, and there are outputs. An example: we might want to calculate the area of a triangle. We’d write a function with inputs base and height, and the output is the area. In Python, this would look like
def triangle_area(base, height):
    return 0.5 * base * height
If we “called” this function and provided values for base and height, it would “return” the area of the triangle. We’ll talk about this structure a lot more in two weeks.
Handle data at engineering scale. A test rig logging 100 readings per second produces 360,000 rows an hour. Excel is not going to help you here. The tools in this course handle that with ease.
Collect and process real engineering data. From a few lines of code you can pull the live position of the International Space Station, read the accelerometer inside your own phone, or send a question to an AI and use its answer inside your program.
Solve the unsolvable. Most real equations in engineering have no analytical solution. Many of those problems can be solved numerically in 10 lines of code.
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
The pipeline
Creating a computational tool looks something like this:

  The computational pipeline
  Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.
  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Idea
    
    Specification
    
    Production
    
    Verification
    
    Use
    
    
    
    
    
    Adaptation
  

The idea is always the hard part. Then, at least for the seventy years after that, production was the bottleneck: writing correct code takes time, and intro courses like this one were traditionally spent almost entirely on how to write correct code.
That era is over. AI tools now produce working code from a good description in seconds. Production has, for most everyday engineering purposes, been solved.


John Backus thought of himself as a bad assembly-language coder, so in the 1950s he created FORTRAN. The history of computer science is a story of making code less abstract, and LLMs might be the next step.
What should be the focus today?
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Specification means describing the problem completely
text:
Specification means describing the problem completely
… the inputs, the outputs, what should happen in between, and what should happen at the edges. It sounds trivial, but it is where real engineering projects most often fail: whether it’s an AI, a contractor, or a teammate who is helping with the task, every gap in your specification gets filled with an assumption. If your specification doesn’t mention a material, maybe the ideal gas assumption is made — problematic when you are talking about oil flowing through a pipeline!
Think about asking a question like…

“Tell me the average temperature in Boulder.”







NoteWhat details do you actually need to provide?





Average over what — the whole century of records, one year, one month? Average of the daily highs, the daily lows, or the midpoint between them (which is what “average temperature” usually means, but maybe you are concerned with human comfort and thus should pay attention to the extremes)? What about the days the weather station didn’t report anything? There are plenty of those if we’re looking back to the 1890s. In the raw file, a missing day might not be blank, it might be recorded as -9999. Hand that to a basic Python program for computing the average and you might “learn” that the average temperature is about −270 °C. And, a classic problem even for humans: What are the units?



Now a different kind of gap. Compare these two problem statements:

A. “Write a function freq_shift(t, U, x0, y0, c, f) that returns the apparent frequency of a moving siren at each time in the array t, and plots it against time.”


B. “Write a program that would allow you to determine the velocity (speed and direction) of a siren.”

Statement A is a completed specification — someone already did all the thinking, and you’re just following instructions. Statement B is a problem. To attack B, you have to decide: what are the inputs my team has access to/ability to control? (A recording? Frequency-vs-time data? Hypothetical object speeds?) What physics connects frequency to velocity? What are the unknowns? What should the program output, and in what form? What if the data is noisy?
In the old version of this course, where we focused on code production, I’d give you Statement A. (Indeed, this was a homework problem last year.) In this version, where we augment our work with LLMs, you might get Statement B. Importantly: in real engineering, no one will hand you Statement A, especially now that LLMs make short work of the ensuing code. Producing Statement A from Statement B is the job.
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
section: Verification means confirming a program does what you intended
text:
Verification means confirming a program does what you intended
… and notably: not assuming that the product given to you by a colleague or LLM is correct. This semester we will verify our code with:
The hand estimate: before running anything, compute a rough expected answer for a simple case. A dropped wrench falls 3 meters in about \(t = \sqrt{2h/g} \approx \sqrt{2(3~\text{m})/(9.8~\text{m/s}^2)} \approx 0.8\) seconds. If the program says 12 seconds, the program is wrong. If it says 0.78 seconds, that’s a good sign.
The edge case: what happens at zero? At a negative input? When the file is empty? What should happen in these cases?
The intuition check: you have years of physical intuition — heavier things don’t fall faster, sirens sound higher approaching than receding, hot coffee cools to room temperature over several minutes but won’t drop below room temperature. That intuition is a verification instrument. Perhaps unexpectedly: we will be practicing our physical intuition in this programming course!






Important



An AI will hand you code that runs yet is confidently, invisibly wrong — it flipped a sign, used the wrong equation because you forgot to specify one, assumed Celsius when the data was in Fahrenheit. It will not warn you. “It ran without errors” and “it is correct” are entirely different claims.
crumbs: What do engineers do with computation?

title: What do engineers do with computation?
text:
The map of this course
Four verbs describe what engineers do with computation, and they outline this course:

Fetch — get real data into (and out of) your programs: sensors, files, the internet.
Process — turn raw data into meaningful quantities: functions, sweeps, big datasets.
Simulate — build models, make predictions, ask “what if,” and know when not to believe yourself.
Analyze — communicate findings honestly: good plots that lead to good understanding, defensible conclusions that lead to engineering decisions.

We’ll spend the most explicit time on Process and Simulate; Fetch and Analyze are woven through everything. The standards page lists what you’ll be able to do under each verb.

On paper (yes, actual paper), write a specification — 5 to 10 sentences — for this problem: a program that tells a student the fastest walking route between two buildings on campus. Your spec must state the inputs, the outputs, and at least three edge cases with what should happen in each.
Class opens with tables exchanging specs and hunting for the gaps.

title: First contact with coding
text: This lesson gets you running Python code in your browser via Google Colab — nothing to install on your computer, nothing to configure, and so we’ll be able to get going very quickly.

text:
Think First
Recall

From last week: what does an LLM do with the gaps in your specification?
We evaluate 2 + 3 * 4 as 14, not 20. What rule is it following, and did anyone ever teach it to you as a computing rule?

Look Ahead

If AI can write code, why are we about to learn to read it line by line?
What’s the difference between a program storing a value and displaying a value?

title: First contact with coding
section: Google Colab: edit code in your browser
text:
Google Colab: edit code in your browser
Go to colab.research.google.com and sign in with your university Google account. Click New notebook. You now have a notebook: a document made of cells, where each cell holds a bit of Python code you can run by pressing Shift+Enter (or the ▶ button).
Type this into the first cell and run it — or, since this page runs Python right here in your browser, you can edit and run the code below (the first run takes a few seconds while Python loads; after that it should be fast):






The text should appear below the cell. The print(...) part is a function (a named, reusable action — much more on these in week 3) whose job is to display the thing between the quotes.

title: First contact with coding
text:
Variables: giving numbers names
A variable is a name attached to a value, so you can use the value by its name:
g = 9.81        # gravitational acceleration, m/s^2
h = 3.0         # drop height, m


The text after a # is a code comment — a note for humans that Python ignores. Here, we described the physical meaning of the variables and included the units of the number.
Variable names can be simple or complex. Probably you will appreciate being able to write a simple, readable equation y=0.5*g*t**2 later in your code, but we also could have defined gravity_earth_surface = 9.81 and then used y=0.5*gravity_earth_surface*t**2 later on.






Tip



It is good practice to make the variable names descriptive such that you know what is going on in the equations involving those variables. Something like g in a mechanics-based program is probably fine because we are so used to seeing g in our mechanics equations. But if we had some code that involved gravity on earth and gravity on the moon (for some reason), it is better to write those as g_earth and g_moon instead of g_1 and g_2.


The = sign here does not mean “equals” in the algebra sense. It means “store the value under this name.” This structure conflicts with our experience in math class, for example:
count = count + 1
If we did algebra on this equation: subtract count from both sides, leaving 0=1… nonsense. But as an instruction, it will take the (current) value of count, add 1, and store the resulting value under the name count (thus replacing the old value stored under that name). This is perfectly acceptable practice, and indeed it is a common ingredient in code.

title: First contact with coding
section: A good habit to get into: predict, then run
text:
A good habit to get into: predict, then run
Here is a complete little program. Before you run it, write down what you expect it to display.






(Sure, you can run it without thinking. I’m not keeping track of what you are doing here… for the sake of your learning, I think you should think! Otherwise this is like the most boring game on the internet: click to see some text.)


** is, annoyingly, Python’s “raise to a power.” So x ** 0.5 is a square root. And * must always be written explicitly: 2h will give an error; you need 2 * h instead.
Some reading help: line 3 computes \(t = \sqrt{2h/g}\), the fall time of an object dropped from height \(h\), subject to gravity \(g\). So: \(2 \times 3 / 9.81 \approx 0.61\), and \(\sqrt{0.61} \approx 0.78\). That is: we predict this code should produce something near 0.78.
Now run it. It should match, unless you changed something in the code. Verification!

title: First contact with coding
text:
Errors are data
In the code above, change t = (2 * h / g) ** 0.5 to t = (2 * h_2 / g) ** 0.5, and run it again. You’ll get an angry red block ending in something like:
NameError: name 'h_2' is not defined
Two things to know about errors:
They are normal. Experts probably do make fewer errors, but they don’t make zero errors… and actually, I use errors as a way to write code faster: just write out a sloppy version of the code without expecting it to work, then: run, read and fix the error; run, read and fix the error; run, read and fix the error; and by then I’m probably done. Read the error messages, they usually describe the error and point to where it occurred in the code. Here: this is a NameError because we used a variable name that the program didn’t know.
They are the friendly failure mode. It is way more difficult to figure out why code runs successfully, but produces a wrong answer. Error messages are kind of nice because they tell you exactly what is wrong (maybe cryptically)!






Tip



Understanding error messages is a genuinely good use of an LLM: paste the code and the full error, and ask what’s wrong. Verify the explanation makes sense — don’t let the LLM do all your thinking for you!

title: First contact with coding
text:
Reading before writing
You now know enough to read simple Python. Predict what this displays before running:












NoteClick for the answer





8 — not 2. Line 2 stored the value 8 under b; it did not create a live mathematical relationship “b is twice a.” When a changed afterward, b is unaware. The code executes top to bottom, each line acting on values as they are at that moment.




On paper, two things:

Your prediction for what this displays with one sentence of reasoning:

x = 10
y = x + 5
x = x + 1
print(x)
print(y)

An electric toothbrush draws about 0.3 A of current (\(I\)) through 4 ohms of resistance (\(R\)); a space heater draws about 12 A through 10 ohms. On paper, set the current and resistance values in the first four lines of your code, then compute and print the power dissipated, \(P = I^2 R\), for both devices. Don’t forget to # comment! Write out your hand estimate on the side. Which device do you expect will dissipate more power?
